newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian stocks seen sliding 100-200 points.
newsitem.headline: Indian stocks seen sliding 100-200 points.

text.p: Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram's miserly handouts are unlikely to boost investor morale and the stock market is seen falling by 100-200 points in the near-term, analysts said on Thursday.
"There's nothing to cheer the moribund market," said broker Ramesh Damani, a member of the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE). "We see strong chances of a downside."

On Wednesday, Chidambaram largely stuck to a new minimum alternate tax (MAT) on companies as he addressed parliament in a debate on the finance bill for 1996/97 (April-March), which disappointed the market.
He made minor adjustments in customs duties which would help some firms like steel and software. The MAT affects firms that avoided tax by ploughing profits into new projects or expansion.

Analysts expect the benchmark 30-stock BSE index falling 100-200 points. "We see the index at 3,000-3,100 levels by December," said M.R. Madhavan, market strategist at ICICI Securities and Finance Company (I-Sec).
The index was trading at 3,354.19 at midsession on Thursday, off 28.52 points or 0.84 percent from the previous close.
"The sops will not boost foreign or retail investors," said V. Nagesh, dealer at Daewoo Securities.
"It was a damp squib," said another dealer at a foreign brokerage. "Matured investors like foreign funds were not expecting MAT to be diluted but I don't see reason for upside."
An expected slowing earnings growth of companies will drag shares down, analysts said.
"Margins are being squeezed," said I-Sec's Madhavan, because overcapacity in some industries made it impossible for them to raise prices to offset rising input costs.
He forecast the earnings growth of firms in the 30-stock BSE index to slow to 17 percent in 1996/97 from 31 percent in 1995/96 and compared to 84 percent in the year before.
"The market is seeking its valuations which is now overpriced," said Shankar Sharma, research head at brokers First Global Finance.

Madhavan said foreign funds, the big buyers in Indian bourses this year, were unlikely to step up purchases because they had already used up their allocations which include cash set apart for buying proposed global depositary receipts issues by Indian companies.

Analysts said retail investors were lured by 16-20 percent interest rates offered by debt instruments. "People are getting disillusioned," said a dealer at UTI Securities. "I don't see shares picking up until the (interest) rates come down."
Peregrine Capital's strategist Ramnath Iyer saw buy opportunities in the slide.
